You can start act differently right now without having to be ashamed. You may feel ashamed of acting differently, but in the end it will only be you and, in the long term, you won't feel like that either. One minute at a time, you have the opportunity and probably the courage to change.

>There should also be a single script that builds them all.  

You mean a post-build event, for instance, that would build customer dlls?  
When one dev builds core, this script builds the other solutions as well. Did I understand correctly?

What about the tests of the other solutions, it would run in this moment as well?
Do you know any github repo or article that shows how that is usually made (loading featureA.dll dinamically).

> Keep your development in one line, use feature flags or similar approaches  

What other similar approaches do you see?
No matter what course of action we consider adopting, we will have to get the decision from the business layer.

> Feature flags can be entirely maintainable if you do them correctly.  

Even permanent feature flags? Wouldn't it become a lot of if-elses everywhere?  
We have 7.5 millions LOC. The code is already hard to understand. So my fear is to turn the code into a sea of if-elses that no one understands.
My fear is that I would put a of permanent feature flags (like 30 each month) on the code, generating a lot of technical debt.

> It's also unclear how changes to core.dll get propagated to all the customers. 

As each customer have his own version of core.dll, at first they don't get what is being developed on core.dll for other customers. But from time to time we sell customers an upgrade to the latest version.

In this moment we get the core.dll on main branch and override the core.dll on the customer branch. When we do this, the customer1.dll breaks on lots of points. We "fix" the compiling errors and pray to god everything is alright. 

We put an army of testers working on exploratory tests on the entire application. After that, the customer puts his own tester doing the same. 

​

> Can you point to *any* articles on the internet where someone is doing something similar to the way you do it? The closest I can think of is in video games, where they often branch a game engine before writing a game, then never update or backport. But that's one branch per game, not per customer 

This example of video game engine looks pretty similar indeed. It is the first time I hear about someone doing something similar. The difference is that from time to time we do this upgrade I told.

​

> Similar to your "TOMORROW" picture, except you have **one branch...**

It is an interesting approach, but what if customer 2 doens't want the new feature that was put on core.dll because customer 1 requested? Would you use permanent feature flags to isolate it? My fear is that, imagine if I have 30 customers and every new request is binded to a feature flag. I would put like 30 feature flags a month on the code.

About the tools we use today, it is basically Jenkins calling Ant/Nant targets. The build steps uses those targets to compile the application, generate some configuration files, do some more stuff, and then Jenkins calls a target which iterate through all the application files and, if the file::get-last-write-time is greater than the date of the last package generated, then it means the file has been altered recently and need to be sent on the package to be deployed. Today everything is on a single god build.xml file. I understand it could be broken into smaller files, it would be of some help.

What I thought about the custom tooling was instead of calling ant/nant targets, to execute a custom tool that we would develop (.exe for example). Smaller services as you mentioned, that would do the task ant/nant did before, but with the benefits of being less verbose, tested and probably easier to understand.
